claim: Enkephalins are opioid peptides that modulate analgesia, reward, and stress.
source: Enkephalins are opioid peptides that modulate analgesia, reward, and stress.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about enkephalins' functions.

claim: In vivo detection of enkephalins remains difficult due to transient and low endogenous concentrations and inherent sequence similarity.
source: In vivo detection of enkephalins remains difficult due to transient and low endogenous concentrations and inherent sequence similarity.
evidence: This statement describes known technical challenges in the field.

claim: The authors previously developed a system combining in vivo optogenetics with microdialysis and a highly sensitive mass spectrometry-based assay to measure opioid peptide release in freely moving rodents.
source: To begin to address this, we previously developed a system combining in vivo optogenetics with microdialysis and a highly sensitive mass spectrometry-based assay to measure opioid peptide release in freely moving rodents (Al-Hasani et al., 2018, eLife).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The current study shows improved detection resolution and stabilization of enkephalin detection.
source: Here, we show improved detection resolution and stabilization of enkephalin detection, which allowed us to investigate enkephalin release during acute stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study presents an analytical method for real-time, simultaneous detection of Met- and Leu-enkephalin in the mouse nucleus accumbens shell after acute stress.
source: We present an analytical method for real-time, simultaneous detection of Met- and Leu-enkephalin (Met-Enk and Leu-Enk) in the mouse nucleus accumbens shell (NAcSh) after acute stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Acute stress activates enkephalinergic neurons in the NAcSh.
source: We confirm that acute stress activates enkephalinergic neurons in the NAcSh using fiber photometry and that this leads to the release of Met- and Leu-Enk.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Acute stress leads to the release of Met- and Leu-Enk in the NAcSh.
source: We confirm that acute stress activates enkephalinergic neurons in the NAcSh using fiber photometry and that this leads to the release of Met- and Leu-Enk.
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis and mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The approach increases spatiotemporal resolution of enkephalin detection.
source: This approach increases spatiotemporal resolution, optimizes the detection of Met-Enk through methionine oxidation, and provides novel insight into the relationship between Met- and Leu-Enk following stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methodological improvements described and demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The approach optimizes the detection of Met-Enk through methionine oxidation.
source: This approach increases spatiotemporal resolution, optimizes the detection of Met-Enk through methionine oxidation, and provides novel insight into the relationship between Met- and Leu-Enk following stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing improved Met-Enk detection after methionine oxidation.

claim: The approach provides novel insight into the relationship between Met- and Leu-Enk following stress.
source: This approach increases spatiotemporal resolution, optimizes the detection of Met-Enk through methionine oxidation, and provides novel insight into the relationship between Met- and Leu-Enk following stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing the 3:1 ratio and differential release patterns.

claim: Endogenous opioid peptides are released at significantly lower concentrations than small molecule neurotransmitters.
source: Endogenous opioid peptides are released at significantly lower concentrations than small molecule neurotransmitters and undergo posttranslational processing that yields ~30 unique peptides from 4 precursor molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about opioid peptide properties.

claim: Endogenous opioid peptides undergo posttranslational processing that yields ~30 unique peptides from 4 precursor molecules.
source: Endogenous opioid peptides are released at significantly lower concentrations than small molecule neurotransmitters and undergo posttranslational processing that yields ~30 unique peptides from 4 precursor molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about opioid peptide processing, supported by citation.

claim: The properties of low concentration and posttranslational processing have made sensitive peptide detection difficult to achieve with existing technologies.
source: Together, these properties have made sensitive peptide detection difficult to achieve with existing technologies (Fricker et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The study shows unique release profiles between Leu- and Met-Enk in response to two different stressors.
source: We show unique release profiles between Leu- and Met-Enk in response to two different stressors and gain new insight into peptide release dynamics; additionally, our method offers improved spatiotemporal resolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data comparing responses to experimenter handling and fox urine.

claim: Enkephalins can act on both the delta and/or mu opioid receptors.
source: Enkephalins can act on both the delta and/or mu opioid receptors, but their activity often depends on receptor and peptide expression patterns, which differ across the brain (Banghart et al., 2018; Gomes et al., 2020; Mansour et al., 1995; Banghart et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Enkephalin activity often depends on receptor and peptide expression patterns, which differ across the brain.
source: Enkephalins can act on both the delta and/or mu opioid receptors, but their activity often depends on receptor and peptide expression patterns, which differ across the brain (Banghart et al., 2018; Gomes et al., 2020; Mansour et al., 1995; Banghart et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In a single brain region, the mu opioid receptor may be activated by an enkephalin or endorphin peptide.
source: For example, in a single brain region, the mu opioid receptor may be activated by an enkephalin or endorphin peptide (Gomes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Any technique that relies on a readout of mu opioid receptor activity is not sufficient to determine whether the peptide is an endorphin or an enkephalin.
source: Therefore, any technique that relies on a readout of mu opioid receptor activity is not sufficient to determine whether the peptide is an endorphin or an enkephalin.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the previous statement about multiple peptides activating the same receptor.

claim: It has been particularly challenging to measure Met- and Leu-Enk selectively and independently in vivo.
source: It has been particularly challenging to measure Met- and Leu-Enk selectively and independently in vivo; in fact, both peptides are typically referred to as 'enkephalins', which oversimplifies their distinct properties.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field and technical challenges.

claim: Both Met- and Leu-Enk are typically referred to as 'enkephalins', which oversimplifies their distinct properties.
source: It has been particularly challenging to measure Met- and Leu-Enk selectively and independently in vivo; in fact, both peptides are typically referred to as 'enkephalins', which oversimplifies their distinct properties.
evidence: This is an observation about nomenclature in the field.

claim: Antibody-based techniques have improved Met- and Leu-Enk detection somewhat.
source: Though antibody-based techniques (Maidment et al., 1989; Marinelli et al., 2005; Hernandez and Hoebel, 1988; Nieto et al., 2002) or liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC-MS) Mabrouk et al., 2011; Li et al., 2009; Baseski et al., 2005 have improved Met- and Leu-Enk detection somewhat, limitations such as spatiotemporal restrictions and poor selectivity between enkephalins remain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC-MS) has improved Met- and Leu-Enk detection somewhat.
source: Though antibody-based techniques (Maidment et al., 1989; Marinelli et al., 2005; Hernandez and Hoebel, 1988; Nieto et al., 2002) or liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC-MS) Mabrouk et al., 2011; Li et al., 2009; Baseski et al., 2005 have improved Met- and Leu-Enk detection somewhat, limitations such as spatiotemporal restrictions and poor selectivity between enkephalins remain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Limitations such as spatiotemporal restrictions and poor selectivity between enkephalins remain in existing detection methods.
source: Though antibody-based techniques (Maidment et al., 1989; Marinelli et al., 2005; Hernandez and Hoebel, 1988; Nieto et al., 2002) or liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC-MS) Mabrouk et al., 2011; Li et al., 2009; Baseski et al., 2005 have improved Met- and Leu-Enk detection somewhat, limitations such as spatiotemporal restrictions and poor selectivity between enkephalins remain.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in existing methods, supported by the context of cited literature.

claim: The authors' group previously developed real-time in vivo detection of evoked opioid peptide release using microdialysis/nanoLC-MS (nLC-MS) after photostimulation.
source: Our group previously developed real-time in vivo detection of evoked opioid peptide release using microdialysis/nanoLC-MS (nLC-MS) after photostimulation (Al-Hasani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: The authors can now selectively measure real-time in vivo levels of basal (non-evoked) peptide release.
source: For the first time, we can selectively measure real-time in vivo levels of basal (non-evoked) peptide release, as well as during behavioral manipulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors can measure peptide release during behavioral manipulations.
source: For the first time, we can selectively measure real-time in vivo levels of basal (non-evoked) peptide release, as well as during behavioral manipulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing peptide release during stress exposures.

claim: The workflow starts with stereotaxic surgery to implant the microdialysis probe in the mouse nucleus accumbens shell (NAcSh).
source: Our workflow (Figure 1A) starts with stereotaxic surgery to implant the microdialysis probe in the mouse nucleus accumbens shell (NAcSh).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The opioid receptor system in the NAcSh mediates both reward and aversion through photostimulation of peptide-expressing neurons across the dorsal/ventral axis.
source: Along with others, we have shown that the opioid receptor system in the NAcSh mediates both reward and aversion through photostimulation of peptide-expressing neurons across the dorsal/ventral axis (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; Pirino et al., 2020; Trieu et al., 2022; Reynolds and Berridge, 2002; Castro and Bruchas, 2019; Schindler et al., 2012; Castro and Berridge, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Custom-made microdialysis probes are intentionally modified to be similar in size to commonly used fiber photometry probes.
source: We use custom-made microdialysis probes, intentionally modified so they are similar in size to commonly used fiber photometry probes, thus causing comparable levels of tissue damage (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the probe design shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The custom microdialysis probes cause comparable levels of tissue damage to fiber photometry probes.
source: We use custom-made microdialysis probes, intentionally modified so they are similar in size to commonly used fiber photometry probes, thus causing comparable levels of tissue damage (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar size of the probes.

claim: The membrane that sits above the brain region of interest is smaller in diameter when compared to a photometry probe.
source: Importantly, the membrane that sits above the brain region of interest is smaller in diameter when compared to a photometry probe (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the probe specifications shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Microdialysis collection occurs every 13 min at a flow rate of 0.8 μL/min.
source: After recovery, we begin microdialysis collection every 13 min, circulating artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) and collecting interstitial fluid (ISF) at a flow rate of 0.8 μL/min.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: A consistent known concentration of isotopically labeled internal standard of Met-Enk and Leu-Enk of 40 amol/sample is added to the collected ISF after each sample collection.
source: After each sample collection, we add a consistent known concentration of isotopically labeled internal standard of Met-Enk and Leu-Enk of 40 amol/sample to the collected ISF for the accurate identification and quantification of endogenous peptide.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The internal standards have a different mass/charge (m/z) ratio than endogenous Met- and Leu-Enk.
source: These internal standards have a different mass/charge (m/z) ratio than endogenous Met- and Leu-Enk.
evidence: This is a description of the internal standard properties.

claim: The variable oxidation of the methionine residue during sample processing results in the signal for Met-Enk being split among multiple m/z values, thereby impairing sensitivity.
source: Importantly, we have resolved one of the main barriers preventing the accurate quantification of Met-Enk: the variable oxidation of the methionine residue during sample processing, which results in the signal for Met-Enk being split among multiple m/z values, thereby impairing sensitivity.
evidence: This is a description of a technical challenge that the authors address.

claim: Converting all methionyl residues to the doubly oxidized sulfone prior to nLC-MS analysis allows for reliable quantification of Met-Enk and differentiation from Leu-Enk without compromising the detection of either peptide.
source: In order to ensure that the signal for Met-Enk is represented by a single m/z value, we converted all methionyl residues to the doubly oxidized sulfone prior to nLC-MS analysis, which allows us to reliably quantify Met-Enk and differentiate it from Leu-Enk without compromising the detection of either peptide (Pesavento et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citation to prior literature on the method.

claim: The methionine oxidation approach represents a key advance and can be applied to any peptide containing a methionine residue.
source: Beyond opioid peptides, this approach represents a key advance and can be applied to any peptide containing a methionine residue.
evidence: This is a generalization based on the chemical properties of the method.

claim: Before the methionine oxidation reaction, Met-Enk can be observed in unoxidized, and singly and doubly oxidized forms with varying intensities.
source: As seen in Figure 1C, before the methionine oxidation reaction at time 0, Met-Enk can be observed in unoxidized, and singly and doubly oxidized forms with varying intensities.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After the methionine oxidation reaction is complete, Met-Enk is observed as doubly oxidized with much higher intensity, enabling accurate quantification.
source: However, after the reaction is complete at time 1, Met-Enk is observed as doubly oxidized with much higher intensity, enabling accurate quantification.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The LLOQ for both Leu-Enk and Met-Enk is 40 amol/sample.
source: We determined that the LLOQ for both Leu-Enk and Met-Enk is 40 amol/sample (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the calibration curve data shown in Figures 1D and E.

claim: The improved quantification limit means increased temporal resolution.
source: The improved quantification limit means increased temporal resolution.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the improved sensitivity.

claim: The current method needs less volume (10 μL or less) and shorter sampling times (10 min or less) compared to previous studies that required 15–20 min.
source: We now need less volume (10 μL or less) and shorter sampling times: 10 min or less, rather than 15–20 min as compared to previous studies (Al-Hasani et al., 2018; DiFeliceantonio et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited prior studies.

claim: High K+ Ringer's solution depolarizes cells and causes the release of dense core vesicles containing neuropeptides.
source: To test the utility of the method in measuring real-time changes in peptide levels in vivo, we evoked the release of the peptides using high K+ Ringer's solution, which depolarizes the cells and causes the release of dense core vesicles containing neuropeptides (Ripley et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: High K+ Ringer's solution significantly increased the release of Met- and Leu-Enk in the NAcSh as compared to baseline.
source: This depolarization state significantly increased the release of Met- and Leu-Enk in the NAcSh as compared to baseline (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Leu-Enk showed a greater fold change compared to baseline than did Met-Enk, with the fold changes being 28 and 7, respectively.
source: Interestingly, Leu-Enk showed a greater fold change compared to baseline than did Met-Enk, with the fold changes being 28 and 7, respectively, based on the data in Figure 1F.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Most past studies reported changes in peptide concentrations as % of baseline rather than raw concentrations.
source: Previous studies reporting opioid peptide measurements rarely represent raw concentrations measured. Instead, most past studies reported changes in peptide concentrations as % of baseline (Mabrouk et al., 2011; Al-Hasani et al., 2018; DiFeliceantonio et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The improved method can detect reliable measurements of both Met- and Leu-Enk at baseline reported as concentrations in the amol/sample range.
source: One key advantage of our improved method is that we can detect reliable measurements of both Met- and Leu-Enk at baseline reported as concentrations in the amol/sample range.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ratio of Met- to Leu-Enk after applying high K+ solution is 3:1 in the NAcSh.
source: We then quantified the ratio of Met- to Leu-Enk after applying high K+ solution and showed that this ratio is 3:1 in the NAcSh (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 1G and H.

claim: The release of Met-Enk is postulated both in vitro and ex vivo to be between three and four times that of Leu-Enk.
source: The release of Met-Enk is postulated both in vitro and ex vivo to be between three and four times that of Leu-Enk (Comb et al., 1982; Hughes et al., 1997; Henderson et al., 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The authors are the first to corroborate the predicted 3:1 ratio in vivo in freely behaving animals, specifically in the NAcSh.
source: We are the first to not only corroborate the predicted ratio in vivo in freely behaving animals, but specifically in the NAcSh.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The 3:1 ratio is almost identical to that previously reported in homogenized human tissue from the sympathoadrenal systems using radioimmunoassays.
source: Interestingly, this 3:1 ratio is almost identical to that previously reported in homogenized human tissue from the sympathoadrenal systems using radioimmunoassays (Yoshimasa et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The conserved ratio highlights the usefulness of rodent models for investigating the highly conserved opioid system and demonstrates its potential in translation to humans.
source: Importantly, this conserved ratio highlights the usefulness of rodent models for investigating the highly conserved opioid system and demonstrates its potential in translation to humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between rodent and human data.

claim: It has been hypothesized that enkephalins act as anti-stress signals based on studies that have shown increased preproenkephalin transcript levels following acute stress.
source: It has been hypothesized that enkephalins act as anti-stress signals based on studies that have shown increased preproenkephalin transcript levels following acute stress (Mansi et al., 2000; Dumont et al., 2000; Ceccatelli and Orazzo, 1993; Valentino and Van Bockstaele, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies using global knockout of enkephalins have shown varying responses to chronic stress interventions.
source: Studies using global knockout of enkephalins have shown varying responses to chronic stress interventions, where male knockout mice showed resistance to chronic mild stress in one study, while another study showed that enkephalin-knockout mice showed delayed termination of corticosteroid release (Melo et al., 2014; Bilkei-Gorzo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Decreased enkephalin expression in the NAc was correlated with an increase in the susceptibility to social defeat.
source: Moreover, decreased enkephalin expression in the NAc was correlated with an increase in the susceptibility to social defeat (Nam et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Enkephalins participate in stress encoding and reactivity.
source: This body of literature supports the hypothesis that enkephalins participate in stress encoding and reactivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: Photostimulation of a subpopulation of peptidergic neurons in the NAcSh drives aversion.
source: Our group has also recently demonstrated that the photostimulation of a subpopulation of peptidergic neurons in the NAcSh drives aversion (Al-Hasani et al., 2015), which further suggests a role for neurons in the NAcSh during aversive stimuli such as stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: It has not been possible to measure the dynamics of real-time peptide release in response to acute stressful stimuli prior to this study.
source: Despite the wealth of data implicating these peptides in the stress response, it has not been possible to measure the dynamics of real-time peptide release in response to acute stressful stimuli.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior methods.

claim: Both Met- and Leu-Enk are released following experimenter handling.
source: We show that both Met- and Leu-Enk are released following experimenter handling, and that the levels decrease within minutes after exposure to the stress (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Enkephalin levels decrease within minutes after exposure to experimenter handling stress.
source: We show that both Met- and Leu-Enk are released following experimenter handling, and that the levels decrease within minutes after exposure to the stress (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No sex differences were found in enkephalin release after experimenter handling after correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: We also analyzed the data with sex as a main effect and did not find any differences between males and females after correcting for multiple comparisons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ratio of 3:1 Met-Enk to Leu-Enk is conserved following experimenter handling.
source: We corroborate our findings from Figure 1G and H showing that the ratio of 3:1 Met-Enk to Leu-Enk is conserved following experimenter handling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Peptide release appears to be precisely controlled.
source: Another key finding is that peptide release appears to be precisely controlled.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of peptide release.

claim: The amount of Met-Enk released at the beginning of the experiment is predictive of later release.
source: We show that the amol/sample of Met-Enk released at the beginning of the experiment is predictive of later release. For example, a higher level released (in the fmol/sample range) during the first collections results in lower levels released (in the amol/sample range) during later collections and vice versa (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a negative correlation (~–0.3) between the first two samples (~26 min) and the later time points, samples 3–10 (~104 min).
source: We show a negative correlation (~–0.3) between the first two samples (~26 min) and the later time points, samples 3–10 (~104 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The negative correlation between early and late Met-Enk release is not due to Met-Enk depletion.
source: Importantly, this relationship is not due to Met-Enk depletion as the circulation of high K+ aCSF is sufficient to drive the release of Met-Enk at the end of an experiment and reverse the negative correlation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The circulation of high K+ aCSF is sufficient to drive the release of Met-Enk at the end of an experiment and reverse the negative correlation.
source: Importantly, this relationship is not due to Met-Enk depletion as the circulation of high K+ aCSF is sufficient to drive the release of Met-Enk at the end of an experiment and reverse the negative correlation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increased calcium activity in enkephalinergic neurons was observed during experimenter handling.
source: During handling, we observed increased calcium activity in enkephalinergic neurons, even after it was repeated twice within a few minutes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Increased calcium activity in enkephalinergic neurons was observed even after handling was repeated twice within a few minutes.
source: During handling, we observed increased calcium activity in enkephalinergic neurons, even after it was repeated twice within a few minutes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Individual responses to experimenter handling varied appreciably.
source: Individual responses to experimenter handling varied appreciably, as shown by the heatmaps and bar plots (Figure 2H and I); such variation could be due to slight differences in probe placement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D) as peptidergic neurons in the dNAcSh encode reward while neurons in the vNAcSh encode aversion (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 2H and I.

claim: Variation in individual responses could be due to slight differences in probe placement.
source: Individual responses to experimenter handling varied appreciably, as shown by the heatmaps and bar plots (Figure 2H and I); such variation could be due to slight differences in probe placement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D) as peptidergic neurons in the dNAcSh encode reward while neurons in the vNAcSh encode aversion (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variation.

claim: Peptidergic neurons in the dNAcSh encode reward while neurons in the vNAcSh encode aversion.
source: Individual responses to experimenter handling varied appreciably, as shown by the heatmaps and bar plots (Figure 2H and I); such variation could be due to slight differences in probe placement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D) as peptidergic neurons in the dNAcSh encode reward while neurons in the vNAcSh encode aversion (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The enkephalin precursor is expressed across the dorsal-ventral axis as shown in the in situ hybridization atlas.
source: Furthermore, the enkephalin precursor is expressed across the dorsal-ventral axis as shown in the in situ hybridization atlas (Allen Brain Institute).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Allen Brain Institute atlas.

claim: The fiber photometry data and peptide release data are concordant, as enkephalinergic neurons are activated following experimenter handling, which drives Met- and Leu-Enk somatodendritic release.
source: The fiber photometry data and peptide release data are concordant, as enkephalinergic neurons are activated following experimenter handling, which drives Met- and Leu-Enk somatodendritic release.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined fiber photometry and microdialysis data.

claim: Repeated neuronal activation may not necessarily lead to repeated peptide release.
source: However, the photometry and peptide release data differ in that repeated neuronal activation may not necessarily lead to repeated peptide release, as suggested by the decrease in peptide release over time in Figure 2D.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fiber photometry cannot provide information about Met- and Leu-Enk independently, as it relies on the precursor gene, Penk.
source: Additionally, fiber photometry cannot provide information about Met- and Leu-Enk independently, as it relies on the precursor gene, Penk.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of fiber photometry.

claim: Fox odor has been widely demonstrated to be aversive to rodents and other mammalian species.
source: Fox odor has been widely demonstrated to be aversive to rodents and other mammalian species (Apfelbach et al., 2005; Endres and Fendt, 2009; Farmer-Dougan et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Predator odor leads to an increase in the expression of the neuronal activation-associated transcription factor fos in enkephalin-positive neurons in different brain regions, including the NAcSh.
source: Prior reports have shown that predator odor leads to an increase in the expression of the neuronal activation-associated transcription factor fos in enkephalin-positive neurons in different brain regions, including the NAcSh (Hebb et al., 2004; Asok et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Upon first exposure to fox urine, the activity of enkephalinergic neurons is markedly increased.
source: We show that upon first exposure, the activity of enkephalinergic neurons is markedly increased (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fiber photometry data shown in Figures 3B–D.

claim: Enkephalinergic activity is significantly attenuated during second and third exposures to fox urine that are separated by 5 min, suggesting habituation to the stimulus.
source: However, this enkephalinergic activity is significantly attenuated during second and third exposures that are separated by 5 min, suggesting habituation to the stimulus (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fiber photometry data shown in Figures 3B–D.

claim: Enkephalinergic neurons also respond to the introduction of a novel object (weigh boat containing water).
source: Interestingly, we show that enkephalinergic neurons also respond to the introduction of a novel object, and the response to the water-containing weigh boat is attenuated upon repeated exposure, which is what we observed for fox urine (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: The response to the water-containing weigh boat is attenuated upon repeated exposure.
source: Interestingly, we show that enkephalinergic neurons also respond to the introduction of a novel object, and the response to the water-containing weigh boat is attenuated upon repeated exposure, which is what we observed for fox urine (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Similar calcium transient responses are observed to both the introduction of a novel object and the odor of a predator, suggesting the same subpopulation of enkephalinergic neurons may have been activated.
source: We compared the enkephalinergic neuron activation in response to both water and fox urine for each individual mouse that experienced both, and we see similar calcium transient responses to both the introduction of a novel object and the odor of a predator, suggesting the same subpopulation of enkephalinergic neurons may have been activated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: A higher level of spiking in the striatum is not always reflected in greater photometry transients.
source: Interestingly and importantly, only recently have researchers shown that a higher level of spiking in the striatum is not always reflected in greater photometry transients (Legaria et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: There is a significant increase in Met-Enk release after exposure to fox odor.
source: In this separate group of animals, we show that there is a significant increase in Met-Enk release after exposure to fox odor (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The response to predator odor varies appreciably: the responses are almost evenly split between elevated release, release with no elevation, or no detectable release.
source: The response to predator odor varies appreciably: the responses are almost evenly split between elevated release, release with no elevation, or no detectable release (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Enkephalins are thought to mediate resilience to stress.
source: Enkephalins are thought to mediate resilience to stress, so the individual differences in responses to predator odor may indicate differences in stress adaptability (Valentino and Van Bockstaele, 2015; Melo et al., 2014; Bérubé et al., 2014; Bérubé et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.
